reason: The narrative demonstrates that non-leaders exercise significant agency throughout. Dinah independently initiates action by going out to see the daughters of the land (v. 1). Jacob's sons—Simeon and Levi—autonomously devise a deceptive strategy and execute a violent response to their sister's violation (vv. 25-27), acting without their father's direction. The men of the city make their own collective decision to accept the circumcision proposal (v. 24). Even among formal leaders, Shechem (though a prince's son) acts on his own desires, and Jacob the patriarch notably responds passively rather than directing events, remaining silent initially. Multiple non-leadership figures take consequential actions that fundamentally shape the narrative, directly contradicting the statement.
